actor: Frontier AI vendor product-security architect owning the user-publishing surface
job: Writing the threat model that treats attacker-published pages on the primary product domain as a reputation-borrowing delivery channel, not a content problem.
outcome: An approved architecture decision relocating user-published pages off the primary product domain onto a separate registrable name.
motivation: Takedowns and upload scanning cannot repair domain reputation, the one asset ad networks and endpoint tooling read as intent.

task.who: Product security and application-security review function
task.what: Draft domain-isolation threat model for the publish surface
task.where: Internal security design review and roadmap prioritization
task.why: Domain reputation is the asset a takedown cannot restore
task.how: Same-site and cookie-boundary analysis against the github.io precedent

actor: Frontier AI vendor platform engineer for the artifact hosting and serving stack
job: Standing up a separate registrable serving domain for published pages, migrating existing artifact URLs and splitting the cookie and same-origin boundary.
outcome: Published pages served from a separate registrable domain that browsers treat as a different site from the product.
motivation: Only a different registrable name stops an untrusted page inheriting the parent's reputation, cookies and same-origin reach.

task.who: Artifact hosting platform and edge-serving engineering team
task.what: Register and cut published-page serving to a new domain
task.where: Edge serving config, DNS, and the publish pipeline
task.why: A separate name cannot borrow the product's reputation
task.how: Public Suffix List submission plus per-page subdomain isolation

actor: Frontier AI vendor trust-and-safety abuse operations lead for publishing features
job: Instrumenting published-page abuse telemetry and building the case that malvertising through the publish feature is structural rather than an isolated campaign.
outcome: A public vendor statement naming abuse, not performance, as the reason published pages moved to a separate domain.
motivation: One campaign drew 7,100 views and hit twenty-nine organizations before takedown; faster takedowns alone do not close the channel.

task.who: Trust and safety abuse operations with security communications
task.what: Quantify publish-feature malvertising abuse and publish the finding
task.where: Abuse telemetry pipeline and the vendor security blog
task.why: A public abuse rationale is what the move requires
task.how: Takedown case data, ad-network reports, redirect-domain registration pivots

actor: Managed-detection threat intelligence researcher tracking malvertising delivery chains
job: Documenting further campaigns that stage payloads behind pages published on AI vendors' own domains, and pivoting on shared registration infrastructure.
outcome: Published research that keeps the publish-to-trusted-domain abuse class visible enough to force a vendor's domain split.
motivation: The security cost stayed theoretical until an operator monetized it; continued documentation is what keeps it priced.

task.who: Threat intelligence and detection engineering research team
task.what: Track and report publish-to-trusted-domain malvertising campaigns
task.where: Incident telemetry across managed endpoint estates, public write-ups
task.why: Documented recurrence turns a theoretical cost into a priced one
task.how: Registrant-email pivots, sponsored-ad destination tracing, sandbox payload analysis

actor: Public Suffix List maintainer reviewing private-section domain submissions
job: Reviewing and merging a vendor's private-section entry so browsers treat the new published-page domain as a distinct site.
outcome: A merged Public Suffix List entry that makes the separate serving domain a real browser-enforced boundary.
motivation: Without the list entry the split is a naming change, not the cookie and same-site boundary the move is for.

task.who: Volunteer list maintainers and submission reviewers
task.what: Review and merge the vendor's private-section domain submission
task.where: The public suffix list repository pull-request queue
task.why: Browser site boundaries follow the list, not the vendor
task.how: Public Suffix List submission and validation process
